chapters.n: Nephi opens the Book of Mormon by introducing himself. He credits his “goodly parents” for teaching him, admits life has been hard, and testifies that God has blessed him richly. That is why he writes.

f.g: Truths that can be known only by revelation.

chapters.n: He writes in his father’s language, combining Jewish learning with Egyptian script or language. Later Book of Mormon writers called their script “reformed Egyptian.”
Nephi bears witness that his record is true, that he engraved it himself, and that he wrote what he personally knew.

f.w: the record which I make is true

chapters.n: The story begins in the first year of King Zedekiah of Judah, around 600 BC. Many prophets—Jeremiah among them—were warning Jerusalem to repent or be destroyed.
Lehi, Nephi’s father, went out and prayed with all his heart for his people. A prophet’s calling often begins with love for others.
As he prayed, a pillar of fire appeared on a rock before him. What he saw and heard made him shake with awe.
Lehi went home and collapsed on his bed, overwhelmed by the Spirit and what he had witnessed.
In vision Lehi saw heaven open and God on His throne, surrounded by countless angels singing praise—much like Isaiah’s throne vision. Alma later quotes this verse word for word.

f.g: Crowds, great gatherings.

chapters.n: He saw One descend from heaven whose brightness exceeded the noonday sun—the premortal Jesus Christ.

f.w: his luster was above that of the sun

chapters.n: Twelve others followed Him, shining brighter than the stars—a preview of Christ’s Twelve Apostles.
They came to earth, and the first one stood before Lehi, handed him a book, and told him to read it. Prophets often receive a book or scroll as part of their call.
As Lehi read, the Spirit of the Lord filled him.
The book announced woe on Jerusalem for its wickedness: it would be destroyed, many would die by the sword, and many would be taken captive to Babylon. This happened in 587/586 BC.

f.g: Woe—a cry of grief and doom.

chapters.n: Despite the grim message, Lehi bursts into praise: God’s works are marvelous, His throne is high, and in His mercy He won’t let those who come to Him perish.

f.w: Great and marvelous are thy works
thou wilt not suffer those who come unto thee that they shall perish

chapters.n: Lehi’s soul rejoiced and his heart was full because of what the Lord showed him.
Nephi explains he won’t give a full account of his father’s visions, dreams, and prophecies. Joseph Smith’s lost 116 pages likely included much of Lehi’s record.
Nephi will summarize his father’s record on plates he made himself, then tell his own story.

f.g: A shortened summary.
Thin metal sheets for engraving durable records.

chapters.n: After his visions, Lehi went among the people and began prophesying about what he had seen and heard, including Jerusalem’s destruction.
People mocked Lehi for exposing their wickedness. He also testified plainly of a coming Messiah and the world’s redemption—Christ is central from the very first chapter.

f.g: Hebrew mashiach — ‘anointed one’; Greek Christos.

chapters.n: The people grew angry and plotted to kill Lehi, as they had done to earlier prophets. Nephi then states a theme of his book: the Lord’s tender mercies strengthen the faithful to be delivered.
In a dream, the Lord blesses Lehi for faithfully delivering His message and warns him that his enemies are trying to kill him.
The Lord commands Lehi in a dream to take his family and leave for the wilderness.
Lehi simply obeys. His prompt obedience is a model for the whole book.
He leaves behind his house, land, gold, silver, and treasures, taking only family, food, and tents. Lehi was apparently wealthy, which makes his sacrifice greater.

f.g: Family land, deeply valued in Israelite law and culture.

chapters.n: The family travels south toward the Red Sea (the Gulf of Aqaba). Nephi names his mother Sariah and his older brothers Laman, Lemuel, and Sam.

f.g: Probably its northeastern arm, the Gulf of Aqaba.

chapters.n: After three days’ travel beyond the Red Sea borders, Lehi pitches his tent in a valley by a river.
Lehi builds a stone altar and offers sacrifice in thanksgiving. As a faithful Israelite, he worships the Lord even in the wilderness.
Lehi names the river after Laman. It flowed into the Red Sea, and the valley lay near its mouth.

f.w: called the name of the river, Laman
f.g: Naming places, as the patriarchs did, was a way to claim and remember.

chapters.n: Seeing the river flow continually into the sea, Lehi pleads with Laman to be like it—constantly flowing toward the source of all righteousness.
He urges Lemuel to be like the valley—firm, steadfast, and immovable in obeying God. This poetic pairing echoes Hebrew style.
Lehi spoke this way because Laman and Lemuel were stubborn. They complained that their “visionary” father had dragged them from home and wealth to die in the desert.

f.g: Stubbornness, like an ox that won’t bend its neck to the yoke.

chapters.n: As the oldest, Laman and Lemuel led the complaining. Nephi’s explanation: they didn’t understand how God works with His children.

f.g: Grumble, complain quietly.

f.w: they knew not the dealings of that God

chapters.n: They didn’t believe the great city of Jerusalem could ever be destroyed. In this they were like the Jerusalemites who wanted their father dead.
Filled with the Spirit, Lehi spoke with such power that his sons physically shook and were silenced, so they obeyed him.

f.g: Silence, put to shame.

chapters.n: A short but meaningful note: Lehi lived in a tent. He had traded a comfortable house for the wilderness at God’s command.
Nephi was young but large in stature and eager to know God’s mysteries. He prayed, and the Lord softened his heart so he believed his father. Even Nephi needed a personal witness.
Nephi shared what the Spirit had shown him with his brother Sam, who believed him.
Laman and Lemuel refused to listen. Grieved by their hard hearts, Nephi prayed for them rather than condemning them.

f.w: I cried unto the Lord for them

chapters.n: The Lord blesses Nephi for seeking Him diligently with humility.

f.g: Humility.

chapters.n: A key promise of the Book of Mormon: keep God’s commandments and you will prosper and be led to a choice land of promise.
The other side of the promise: if his brothers rebel, they will be cut off from the Lord’s presence.

f.w: cut off from the presence of the Lord

chapters.n: If Nephi stays faithful, he will become a ruler and teacher over his brothers—echoing the story of Joseph and his older brothers.

When the brothers rebel, the Lord will curse them, and they will have no power over Nephi’s descendants unless those descendants also rebel. In the Book of Mormon, the heart of the curse is separation from God’s presence.
If Nephi’s people rebel, their brothers’ descendants will become a “scourge” to stir them up to remember God. Hardship can be a call back to Him.

f.g: A whip—here a source of affliction meant to prompt repentance.

chapters.n: Nephi returns to his father’s tent after his experience of prayer with the Lord (chapter 2).
Lehi says the Lord has commanded in a dream that Nephi and his brothers go back to Jerusalem—a dangerous trip of several hundred miles.
The reason: a man named Laban holds the record of the Jews and Lehi’s family genealogy, engraved on plates of brass.

f.g: A powerful man in Jerusalem, apparently a military officer and relative of Lehi.

chapters.n: The Lord wants the brothers to go to Laban’s house, get the records, and bring them back to the wilderness.
Lehi notes that Laman and Lemuel are already complaining that it’s too hard—but he reminds Nephi this is the Lord’s command, not just his own.
Lehi tells Nephi to go, promising that the Lord will favor him because he hasn’t complained.
Nephi’s famous answer: “I will go and do,” because the Lord never gives a commandment without preparing a way to keep it. This verse has become a motto of faith-driven obedience.
Lehi is overjoyed, recognizing that the Lord has blessed Nephi.
The four brothers travel back through the wilderness with their tents toward Jerusalem.

f.g: Travel to Jerusalem was always ‘up’ because the city sits in the hills.

chapters.n: Arriving near Jerusalem, the brothers discuss how to approach Laban.

f.g: Discuss, take counsel together.

chapters.n: They cast lots to decide who should go, a common ancient way to seek God’s choice. The lot falls on Laman, who visits Laban at his house.
Laman asks Laban for the brass plates containing their family’s genealogy.
Laban angrily throws him out, refuses to give the records, calls him a robber, and threatens to kill him.

f.g: An accusation that could carry a death penalty.

chapters.n: Laman escapes and reports back. Discouraged, the brothers are ready to give up and return to their father.
Nephi makes a solemn oath: they won’t return until they’ve done what the Lord commanded.

f.w: As the Lord liveth, and as we live
f.g: A Hebrew oath formula of the strongest kind.

chapters.n: He proposes a new plan: go to their family’s estate and collect the gold, silver, and riches Lehi left behind to trade for the plates.
Nephi explains that Lehi left everything because he knew Jerusalem would be destroyed for its wickedness.
The people rejected the prophets, so staying would have meant dying with them. Lehi had to flee.

f.w: rejected the words of the prophets

chapters.n: Nephi explains why the plates matter: God wisely wants them to preserve their ancestors’ language for their children.

f.w: preserve unto our children the language

chapters.n: The plates also preserve the words of all the holy prophets since the world began. Without scripture, a people can lose both its faith and its identity.

f.w: words which have been spoken by the mouth of all the holy prophets

chapters.n: With these arguments Nephi persuades his brothers to keep trying.
They go to their family estate and gather their gold, silver, and valuables.
Then they return to Laban’s house with their treasure.
They offer Laban all their wealth in exchange for the brass plates.
Seeing their great wealth, Laban greedily wants it all. He throws them out and sends servants to kill them so he can keep the property.
The brothers run for their lives, forced to leave their riches behind with Laban.
They escape into the wilderness and hide in a cave or hollow in the rock.

f.g: A cave or cleft; the Judean hills are full of them.

chapters.n: Angry at Nephi and Lehi, Laman—joined by Lemuel—insults Nephi and Sam and starts beating them with a stick.

f.w: smite us even with a rod
f.g: Beat with a stick or staff.

chapters.n: An angel suddenly appears and rebukes them: the Lord has chosen Nephi to lead because of their wickedness. Go back to Jerusalem; the Lord will deliver Laban into your hands.

f.w: chosen him to be a ruler over you

chapters.n: Having delivered his message, the angel leaves.
Even after seeing an angel, Laman and Lemuel complain again: Laban is powerful and commands fifty men—how could the Lord deliver him to us? A miracle alone doesn’t create faith.

f.g: Laban seems to have been a military commander.

chapters.n: Nephi answers his brothers’ fear with logic of faith: God is mightier than the whole earth, so surely He is mightier than Laban and his fifty—or even tens of thousands.
He points to Moses: at the Lord’s command the Red Sea parted, Israel crossed on dry ground, and Pharaoh’s army drowned. The Exodus is a pattern for their own deliverance.
You know this is true, Nephi says, and you’ve just seen an angel—so why doubt? The Lord can deliver us as He did our fathers.
Still angry and grumbling, the brothers nonetheless follow Nephi to just outside Jerusalem’s walls.

f.g: Angry.

chapters.n: It is night. Nephi has his brothers hide outside the walls while he slips into the city toward Laban’s house.
A verse loved by many: Nephi was led by the Spirit without knowing in advance what he would do. Faith often means taking the next step before seeing the whole path.
Approaching Laban’s house, Nephi finds a man collapsed on the ground, drunk.

f.g: Laban had been out at night with the elders of the Jews (v. 22).

chapters.n: The drunk man turns out to be Laban himself.

Nephi draws Laban’s sword and admires it: a gold hilt, fine craftsmanship, and a blade of precious steel. Nephi later uses it as a pattern for making swords, and it is passed down through the generations.
The Spirit urges Nephi to kill Laban, but he recoils—he has never killed anyone. His reluctance shows his tender conscience.

f.g: Strongly urged or compelled.
Drew back in horror.

chapters.n: The Spirit says again that the Lord has delivered Laban into his hands. Nephi weighs the facts: Laban tried to kill him, rejected God’s commandments, and stole their property.
A third time, the Spirit commands Nephi to slay Laban.

The Spirit explains: the Lord sometimes takes the wicked to fulfill His righteous purposes. Better that one man die than a whole nation dwindle in unbelief. This was a unique, divinely directed exception, not a pattern for others.

f.w: better that one man should perish

chapters.n: Nephi remembers the Lord’s promise that his descendants would prosper if they kept the commandments.

f.w: they shall prosper in the land of promise

chapters.n: He reasons that his people couldn’t keep the law of Moses if they didn’t have it.
And the law was recorded on the brass plates.

f.w: engraven upon the plates of brass

chapters.n: Nephi concludes that the Lord delivered Laban to him so he could obtain the records as commanded.
Nephi obeys the Spirit and kills Laban with his own sword. Like David taking Goliath’s head with the giant’s own sword, the enemy’s weapon becomes his downfall.

f.w: smote off his head with his own sword

chapters.n: Nephi puts on Laban’s clothes and armor so he can pass as Laban.

f.g: Every bit, completely.

chapters.n: Heading to Laban’s treasury, Nephi meets the servant with the keys and orders him in Laban’s voice to come with him.

f.g: A storeroom for valuables and records.

chapters.n: The servant believes Nephi is his master because of the clothing and sword.
The servant chats about the elders of the Jews, since he knew Laban had spent the night with them.

f.g: Leading men of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Nephi speaks to him as if he were Laban.
He tells the servant he must take the brass plates to his “elder brethren” outside the walls.

f.g: The engraved record on the plates.

chapters.n: Nephi tells the servant to follow him.
The servant assumes Nephi means fellow church leaders—“brethren of the church”—and follows.

f.g: The Book of Mormon uses ‘church’ for the community of believers even before Christ.

chapters.n: As they walk, the servant keeps talking about the elders of the Jews.
Seeing someone who looks like Laban approaching, Laman, Lemuel, and Sam panic and run, thinking Nephi has been killed and they’re next.
Nephi calls out, and recognizing his voice, they stop running.
When the servant sees the brothers, he realizes something is wrong and starts to flee back to the city.
Nephi, large and strengthened by the Lord, grabs the servant and holds him.
Nephi swears by the Lord’s life and his own that they will spare the servant if he listens.

f.w: as the Lord liveth, and as I live

chapters.n: He promises with an oath that the servant can be a free man like them if he joins them in the wilderness.
Nephi explains that the Lord commanded this and asks, shouldn’t we be diligent in obeying Him? If the servant comes, he will have a place among them.
The servant, named Zoram, takes courage and swears an oath to stay with them from then on. Oaths were deeply binding in that culture, and his descendants became the Zoramites.
They wanted Zoram to stay so Jerusalem wouldn’t learn of their escape and chase them.
Once Zoram swore his oath, their fears about him ended—they trusted his word.

f.g: Shows how sacred and binding an oath was.

chapters.n: They take the brass plates and Zoram and return to Lehi’s tent in the wilderness. The mission is accomplished.
When the sons return, Lehi is filled with joy, and Sariah is overjoyed—she had been grieving, fearing they were dead.
Thinking her sons had died in the wilderness, Sariah had complained to Lehi, calling him a visionary man who had led them from their home to lose their sons and perish.

f.g: Someone who sees visions—here used as a complaint, as Laman and Lemuel had.

chapters.n: Nephi frankly records his mother’s complaints. Even faithful people struggle under fear and grief.
Lehi gently embraces the label: yes, he is a visionary man. Without visions he wouldn’t have known God’s goodness and would have died with others in Jerusalem.

f.w: I know that I am a visionary man

chapters.n: He testifies that he has obtained a land of promise, and he knows the Lord will bring their sons safely back.
Lehi comforted Sariah this way while the sons were away on their errand.
When they arrived, their joy was full, and Sariah was comforted.
Sariah bears her own testimony: now she knows for certain the Lord commanded Lehi to flee and protected her sons. Faith tested by trial became sure knowledge.

f.w: Now I know of a surety

chapters.n: The family rejoices and offers sacrifices and burnt offerings, thanking the God of Israel.
After giving thanks, Lehi starts studying the brass plates from the beginning—scripture study as a family priority.
The plates included the five books of Moses—Genesis through Deuteronomy—recording the Creation and Adam and Eve, our first parents.

f.g: The Torah or Pentateuch.

chapters.n: They also contained Jewish history from the beginning up to the start of Zedekiah’s reign.
And prophecies of the holy prophets, including many from Jeremiah, Lehi’s contemporary. The brass plates also held prophecies by Zenos, Zenock, and Neum that are not in our Bible.
Lehi found his genealogy and learned he descended from Joseph, Jacob’s son, who was sold into Egypt and preserved by God to save his family from famine. Later we learn Lehi was of Manasseh.
The same God later led Israel out of Egyptian slavery. Lehi’s family sees its own journey in that story.

f.w: out of the land of Egypt

chapters.n: So Lehi discovered his ancestry. Laban was also descended from Joseph, which explains why his family kept the records.

f.w: Laban also was a descendant of Joseph
f.g: Suggests the plates were a family record of a Joseph line in Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Filled with the Spirit, Lehi began to prophesy about his descendants.
He foretold that the brass plates would go forth to all nations, families, languages, and peoples of his descendants.
He prophesied that the plates would never perish or be dimmed by time—and he said many other things about his posterity.
Nephi notes that so far he and his father have kept the Lord’s commandments.
They had obtained the records, searched them, and found them precious, because they would help preserve the Lord’s commandments for their children.
So it was wise of the Lord to have them carry the records on their journey to the promised land.
Nephi pauses to explain his record. He won’t include his family genealogy in these plates, since his father’s record already has it.

f.g: The small plates of Nephi, focused on sacred things.

chapters.n: It is enough to say they descend from Joseph.
He won’t try to record everything about his father, because he wants the limited space on the plates for the things of God.
Nephi states his whole purpose: to persuade everyone to come to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and be saved. This is the mission of the entire Book of Mormon.

f.w: persuade men to come unto the God of Abraham

chapters.n: So he writes not what pleases the world, but what pleases God and those not caught up in worldliness.
Nephi will instruct his descendants not to fill these plates with things that aren’t valuable to people’s souls. His successors followed this counsel.
After Lehi’s prophecies, the Lord tells him his family shouldn’t go into the wilderness alone. His sons need wives so they can raise up children unto the Lord in the promised land.

f.w: raise up seed unto the Lord

f.g: Fitting, appropriate.

chapters.n: So the Lord commands Nephi and his brothers to return to Jerusalem and bring Ishmael and his family into the wilderness.

f.g: A man in Jerusalem, apparently already close to Lehi’s family.

chapters.n: Once again, Nephi and his brothers make the long journey back toward Jerusalem.
They reach Ishmael’s house, gain his trust, and share the Lord’s message with him.
The Lord softens the hearts of Ishmael and his household, and they all travel back with the brothers toward Lehi’s tent. This second trip goes far more smoothly than the first.
On the way, Laman, Lemuel, two of Ishmael’s daughters, and Ishmael’s two sons and their families rebel against Nephi, Sam, Ishmael, his wife, and their other three daughters.
The rebels want to go back to Jerusalem.

f.w: return unto the land of Jerusalem

chapters.n: Grieved by their hard hearts, Nephi asks his older brothers why they are so hardened and blind that their younger brother must teach them and set the example.
Why haven’t you listened to the Lord’s word?
How could you forget that you saw an angel?
How could you forget the great things the Lord did in rescuing us from Laban and giving us the record? Forgetting God’s blessings is a recurring danger in the Book of Mormon.

f.w: how is it that ye have forgotten

chapters.n: And how could you forget that the Lord can do anything according to His will for those who have faith in Him? So let’s be faithful.

f.w: the Lord is able to do all things

chapters.n: If we’re faithful, we’ll reach the promised land—and you’ll eventually see that the prophecies of Jerusalem’s destruction come true.
The Lord’s Spirit will soon stop striving with Jerusalem’s people. They rejected the prophets, imprisoned Jeremiah, and tried to kill Lehi, driving him away.

f.w: Jeremiah have they cast into prison

chapters.n: If you go back to Jerusalem, you’ll perish with them. You’re free to choose—but remember my warning. Nephi says the Spirit compels him to say this.
Enraged, the rebels grab Nephi and tie him up with ropes, meaning to leave him to be eaten by wild animals.
Nephi prays: according to my faith in you, deliver me—give me strength to break these ropes.
The ropes fall from his hands and feet, and he stands and speaks to them again. The Lord answered his prayer, though not exactly in the way he asked.
The rebels again try to seize him, but one of Ishmael’s daughters, her mother, and one of Ishmael’s sons plead for Nephi until the brothers soften and stop trying to kill him.

f.g: Women in the family act as peacemakers here.

chapters.n: Sorry for their wickedness, the brothers bow before Nephi and beg his forgiveness—another echo of Joseph’s brothers bowing to him.
Nephi freely forgives them and urges them to pray for the Lord’s forgiveness, which they do. Then they continue toward Lehi’s tent.

f.g: frankly = freely, generously.

chapters.n: Arriving at Lehi’s tent, everyone gives thanks to the Lord and offers sacrifices and burnt offerings.
Preparing for the long journey, the family gathers seeds of every kind—grain and fruit—to plant in the promised land.
While camped in the wilderness, Lehi tells his family he has had a dream—or, as he clarifies, a vision. This is the famous vision of the tree of life.
Because of what he saw, Lehi rejoices over Nephi and Sam, believing they and many of their descendants will be saved.
But he fears greatly for Laman and Lemuel. The vision began in a dark and dreary wilderness.

f.g: It seemed to me.
A picture of the fallen world without God’s light.

chapters.n: A man dressed in a white robe came and stood before Lehi—a heavenly guide.
The man told Lehi to follow him.
Following him, Lehi found himself in a dark and dreary wasteland.
After walking many hours in darkness, Lehi prayed for the Lord’s mercy. Prayer is the turning point—light comes after he cries to God.
After praying, Lehi saw a large and spacious field.
He saw a tree whose fruit was desirable to make people happy. Nephi later learns the tree represents the love of God, shown supremely in Jesus Christ.
Lehi ate the fruit and found it sweeter than anything he had ever tasted, and whiter than any whiteness he had seen—purity and joy beyond comparison.
The fruit filled his soul with great joy, and his first thought was for his family to taste it too. True conversion naturally turns outward toward loved ones.

f.w: desirous that my family should partake

chapters.n: Looking around for his family, Lehi saw a river running near the tree.

f.g: Nephi learns it represents filthiness and the depths of hell.

chapters.n: At the river’s head he saw Sariah, Sam, and Nephi standing uncertain, as if they didn’t know where to go.
Lehi beckoned and called loudly for them to come and eat the fruit, which was more desirable than any other.
They came and ate the fruit too.
Lehi longed for Laman and Lemuel to come as well, so he looked toward the river’s head to find them.
He saw them, but they refused to come and eat. Even God’s love does not override agency.
Lehi saw a rod of iron running along the riverbank to the tree. Nephi learns the rod is the word of God, which leads to the love of God.
He also saw a strait and narrow path running beside the rod to the tree, passing the head of the fountain to a large field that seemed like a world. “Strait” means tight or restricted.

f.g: strait = narrow, confined—not ‘straight.’

chapters.n: Countless crowds were pushing forward, trying to reach the path to the tree.
They came and started on the path.
Then a thick mist of darkness arose, and many who had started on the path lost their way, wandered off, and were lost. Nephi learns the mist represents the devil’s temptations.
Others pressed forward, grabbed the end of the rod of iron, and clung to it through the mist until they reached the tree and ate the fruit. Holding to God’s word gets us through temptation.

f.w: clinging to the rod of iron

chapters.n: Yet after eating the fruit, some looked around as if they were ashamed. Reaching the tree is not the end of the test.
Across the river Lehi saw a great and spacious building, standing as if in the air, high above the earth—impressive but without foundation.

f.g: Represents the pride of the world and its vain imaginations.

chapters.n: It was full of people, young and old, men and women, dressed in very fine clothes, mocking and pointing at those eating the fruit.

f.w: manner of dress was exceedingly fine

chapters.n: Embarrassed by the mockery, some who had tasted the fruit wandered into forbidden paths and were lost. Peer pressure can pull people from what they know is good.
Nephi notes he isn’t recording all of his father’s words.

In brief: Lehi saw other crowds who grabbed the rod and kept pressing forward, continually holding fast, until they reached the tree, fell down in worship, and ate. “Continually holding fast” is the key difference from verse 24.

f.w: continually holding fast to the rod of iron

f.g: A posture of worship and humility.

chapters.n: He also saw crowds feeling their way toward the great and spacious building.

f.g: Groping, as in darkness.

chapters.n: Many drowned in the depths of the fountain, and many disappeared, wandering on strange roads.
A great crowd entered the strange building and pointed scornfully at Lehi and those eating the fruit—but they ignored the mockers.
Lehi’s words: everyone who paid attention to the mockers fell away.
Sadly, Lehi says, Laman and Lemuel never ate the fruit.
After describing his vision, Lehi says he greatly fears Laman and Lemuel will be cast off from the Lord’s presence.

f.w: cast off from the presence of the Lord

chapters.n: With all the feeling of a tender parent, Lehi pleads with them to listen, hoping the Lord will be merciful and not cast them off.

f.w: with all the feeling of a tender parent

chapters.n: After preaching and prophesying many things, he urged them to keep the Lord’s commandments, and then stopped speaking.
Lehi saw, heard, and taught all these things while living in a tent in the valley of Lemuel—far more than Nephi can write on these plates.
Nephi explains that he keeps two sets of plates, both called the plates of Nephi. One—the large plates—holds the full history of his people.
The Lord commanded him to make these plates—the small plates—especially to record the ministry, the spiritual history of his people.
The other plates are mostly for the reigns of kings, wars, and conflicts; these small plates are mostly for sacred matters.
The Lord commanded Nephi to make these plates for a wise purpose that he didn’t know. About 2,400 years later, these plates replaced the 116 manuscript pages Joseph Smith lost.
Nephi trusts that the Lord knows all things from the beginning, prepares a way to accomplish His work, and has all power to fulfill His words.

f.w: the Lord knoweth all things from the beginning

chapters.n: Nephi turns from his father’s dream to a new section of his record. He calls it an account of his own “reign and ministry,” written years later after he had become the Nephites’ leader, but he must first finish telling of Lehi and his brothers.

f.g: The small plates of Nephi, a record set apart for sacred things.

chapters.n: After describing the tree of life dream, Lehi urged his family to be diligent and then began to prophesy about the Jews back in Jerusalem.

Lehi foresees Jerusalem’s destruction and the Babylonian captivity, then the Jews’ return to their homeland. This happened: Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587/586 BC, and Persia’s King Cyrus let the exiles go home about fifty years later.

Lehi gives a precise timeline: the Messiah would come six hundred years after he left Jerusalem. The title “Messiah” means “anointed one,” and Lehi immediately explains it in plain terms — the Savior of the whole world.

f.g: Hebrew mashiaḥ, “anointed one”; in Greek, Christos.

chapters.n: Lehi points out that he was not alone: many prophets before him had testified of this coming Redeemer. Testimony of Christ runs through all of scripture.

f.w: how great a number had testified

chapters.n: This is why a Redeemer is needed: since the Fall, all people are lost and fallen, and they would stay that way forever unless they rely on Him. It is a short, clear statement of the core of the plan of salvation.

f.w: lost and in a fallen state

chapters.n: Lehi also prophesies of a forerunner who would prepare people for the Messiah — the one we know as John the Baptist.

f.w: prepare the way of the Lord

chapters.n: Lehi’s words closely match what John the Baptist would actually say six centuries later. A shoe’s “latchet” is its strap; untying a master’s sandals was a servant’s lowliest job, so John is saying he isn’t worthy even to be Christ’s humblest servant.

f.g: The leather strap or thong of a sandal.

chapters.n: Lehi even names the place: Bethabara, east of the Jordan River, which is where the Gospel of John says John was baptizing. The prophecy also foresees John baptizing Jesus Himself.

f.g: A crossing place on the Jordan; some manuscripts of John 1:28 read “Bethany beyond Jordan.”

chapters.n: After baptizing Jesus, John would testify that He is the “Lamb of God” — a title that recalls the lambs offered in sacrifice and points to Christ’s atoning death for the sins of the world.
Lehi foresees the gospel being preached to the Jews, their rejection of Jesus, His death and resurrection, and then the message going to the Gentiles (non-Israelites) through the Holy Ghost.

f.w: dwindling of the Jews in unbelief
manifest, by the Holy Ghost, unto the Gentiles

chapters.n: Lehi uses an olive tree to picture Israel. Its branches broken off and scattered represent Israelite groups — including Lehi’s own family — being separated from the main body of the covenant people.
Lehi sees his family’s journey to a new land as part of this scattering. Their departure is not random; it fulfills God’s plan for scattering Israel throughout the world.

The scattering is not the end of the story. After the Gentiles receive the full gospel, the “natural branches” — remnants of Israel — will be grafted back in by coming to know Jesus as their true Messiah. This is the gathering of Israel.

f.g: In short; to sum up.

chapters.n: Nephi notes that Lehi said much more than he records here. Nephi had written more of it in his “other book,” the large plates, which focused on history.

f.g: The large plates of Nephi, the more historical record.

chapters.n: All of this teaching took place in the family’s tent camp in the valley of Lemuel, near the Red Sea, early in their journey.

Nephi longs to see and know for himself what his father saw. He explains that Lehi received revelation by the Holy Ghost through faith in Christ, and that this same gift is open to everyone who diligently seeks God.

f.w: desirous also that I might see

chapters.n: God does not change. Because He is the same in every age, the path back to Him has been prepared for all people from the beginning, on the same condition: repent and come to Him.

f.w: the same yesterday, today, and forever
from the foundation of the world

chapters.n: Whoever seeks diligently will find. God’s “mysteries” — truths known only by revelation — are opened by the Holy Ghost in every era. The phrase “one eternal round” means God’s ways are consistent; He doesn’t play favorites across time.

f.w: he that diligently seeketh shall find

chapters.n: Nephi turns to address his reader directly: everything we do will one day be judged.
Mortal life is a “probation,” a testing period. Those who choose wickedness and do not repent will be unclean at the judgment, and nothing unclean can live in God’s presence.

f.g: The time of testing in mortality.

f.w: no unclean thing can dwell with God

chapters.n: Nephi closes by explaining why he speaks so boldly: the Holy Ghost has given him authority to say these things, and he will not deny them.

Nephi’s vision begins with three things: he wanted to know, he believed God could show him, and he sat pondering. In that moment he was carried away in the Spirit to a very high mountain — a classic setting for revelation in scripture.
The Spirit begins with a question. God often invites us to state what we really want before He teaches us.
Nephi’s answer is simple and direct: he wants to see what his father saw.

f.w: the things which my father saw

chapters.n: The Spirit tests Nephi’s faith with a second question: does he believe Lehi really saw the tree?
Nephi affirms that he believes all his father’s words. His faith in a living prophet becomes the doorway to his own revelation.

f.w: I believe all the words of my father

chapters.n: The Spirit bursts into praise. “Hosanna” is a Hebrew cry meaning “save, please,” used as a shout of worship. Nephi is blessed because he believes in the Son of God, and he is promised he will see what he asked for.

f.g: From Hebrew hoshi‘ah na, “save now, please”; a shout of praise.

chapters.n: Nephi is told he will see more than the tree: he will witness a man coming down from heaven, and then bear record that this man is the Son of God. The vision of the tree will lead to the vision of Christ.

f.w: a man descending out of heaven

chapters.n: Nephi sees the tree, even more beautiful than he imagined. Its brilliant whiteness suggests purity and holiness.
Nephi recognizes that this tree is more precious than anything else.
The Spirit asks again what Nephi wants, inviting him to go deeper.

Nephi asks for the meaning of the tree. He notes that the Spirit of the Lord appeared in the form of a man and spoke with him person to person. Latter-day Saints understand this as a rare record of the Holy Ghost, a personage of spirit, appearing in human form.

f.w: in the form of a man
as a man speaketh with another

chapters.n: When Nephi turns to look at his guide, the Spirit is gone. The vision now shifts to a new scene.
Rather than explaining the tree with words, the vision shows Nephi Jerusalem, then the town of Nazareth, and a young virgin there — Mary. Nephi sees her purity and beauty.
An angel now becomes Nephi’s guide for the rest of the vision, and starts with a question about what Nephi sees.
Nephi describes Mary as the most beautiful and fair of all virgins — honoring her unique role.

The angel asks a key question. “Condescension” means coming down from a high place to a lowly one. The vision will show how God Himself — both the Father in sending His Son and the Son in coming — stooped to enter mortal life.

f.g: Descending from divine glory to humble mortal circumstances.

chapters.n: Nephi’s honest reply is a model of humble faith: he knows God loves His children, even though he doesn’t understand everything.

f.w: I know that he loveth his children

chapters.n: The angel explains that Mary would be the mother of the Son of God “after the manner of the flesh” — Jesus would have a mortal mother and an immortal Father.

f.w: after the manner of the flesh

chapters.n: Mary is “carried away in the Spirit” for a time — a reverent, unexplained reference to the miraculous conception of Jesus.
Nephi now sees Mary holding a baby. The Son of God has been born.

f.w: bearing a child in her arms

chapters.n: The angel declares the child to be the Lamb of God and Son of the Eternal Father, then asks whether Nephi now understands the tree. The answer is shown, not just told: the gift of the infant Christ is the meaning of the tree.

f.w: the Son of the Eternal Father

chapters.n: Nephi understands: the tree is the love of God, poured into people’s hearts — and that love is shown supremely in the gift of His Son. That is why it is more desirable than anything else.

f.g: Pours out and spreads widely.

chapters.n: The angel adds that God’s love is not only most desirable but also the most joyful thing a soul can experience — echoing Lehi’s description of the fruit filling his soul with joy.
Nephi sees Jesus as an adult moving among people during His ministry, and many falling at His feet to worship Him.

f.w: fall down at his feet and worship him

chapters.n: Nephi learns more symbols: the iron rod is the word of God, which leads to the fountain of living waters and to the tree of life. Both the waters and the tree represent God’s love.
The angel again invites Nephi to look at the “condescension of God” — now focusing on the Son Himself and the humble path He would take.

Nephi sees Jesus baptized by John the Baptist, the heavens opened, and the Holy Ghost descending in the form of a dove. This matches the Gospel accounts closely, written six centuries before the event.

f.g: The dove is a sign; the Holy Ghost Himself is not a dove.

f.w: the prophet who should prepare the way

chapters.n: Jesus ministers with power and draws large crowds, yet many reject Him and cast Him out.

f.w: they cast him out from among them

chapters.n: Nephi sees twelve disciples following Jesus — the Twelve Apostles. Then they are removed from his view.
Nephi sees angels coming down to minister to people — heaven reaching earth during Christ’s mortal ministry.

f.w: angels descending upon the children of men

chapters.n: Nephi sees Jesus healing the sick and casting out evil spirits by His own power — miracles that showed who He was.

f.w: they were healed by the power of the Lamb of God

chapters.n: Nephi sees Jesus arrested and judged by the world. Here the condescension reaches its depth: the Son of the everlasting God submits to the judgment of men.
Nephi witnesses the Crucifixion. Jesus was lifted up on the cross and died for the sins of the world.
After Christ’s death, Nephi sees the world gathering to fight against His apostles. The angel explains that the Twelve are called “apostles of the Lamb.”
The opposition gathers in a great and spacious building like the one in Lehi’s dream. The angel calls it “the world and the wisdom thereof,” and notes that many in Israel itself fought the Twelve.
Nephi learns the building represents the pride of the world, and he sees it fall with a great crash. All who fight against the Lamb’s apostles will eventually fall the same way.

f.w: the fall thereof was exceedingly great

chapters.n: The vision turns to Nephi’s own future. The angel shows him the promised land filled with his descendants and those of his brothers — so many they seem like the sand of the sea, echoing God’s promise to Abraham.

f.w: as many as the sand of the sea

chapters.n: Nephi sees battles, threats of war, and great bloodshed among his people. The Book of Mormon will record much of this conflict.
Generation after generation passes amid war and contention, and the land fills with more cities than Nephi can count.
Nephi foresees the catastrophic storms, earthquakes, fires, and sinking cities that would strike the promised land at the time of Christ’s death. Six centuries later, 3 Nephi records exactly this.

f.w: many cities that they were sunk

chapters.n: After the darkness lifts, Nephi sees that many people survived those terrible judgments — the more righteous, as 3 Nephi later explains.
This is the high point of Book of Mormon history: the resurrected Jesus Christ descending from heaven and showing Himself to Nephi’s descendants.

f.w: the Lamb of God descending out of heaven

chapters.n: Nephi sees the Holy Ghost come upon twelve chosen disciples in the Americas, ordained by God.
The angel identifies them as the twelve disciples who would minister to Nephi’s descendants.

The angel describes an order of judgment: the Twelve Apostles in Jerusalem will judge the twelve tribes of Israel, and since Lehi’s family is of Israel, the Nephite twelve will themselves be judged by those apostles.

f.w: judge the twelve tribes of Israel

chapters.n: The Nephite twelve will judge Nephi’s descendants. They are called righteous forever because their faith in Christ has made their “garments white in his blood” — a vivid image of being cleansed by the Atonement.

f.w: their garments are made white in his blood

chapters.n: Nephi sees three generations after Christ’s visit live in righteousness. They too are made clean through faith in the Lamb. 4 Nephi describes this remarkable era of peace.

f.w: three generations pass away in righteousness

chapters.n: Many in the fourth generation also remain righteous — but this hints that the decline will begin then.
The scene shifts again to great gatherings of people — a sign that conflict is coming.
The angel directs Nephi to look at both his descendants and his brothers’ descendants.

f.g: The Lamanites, descendants of Laman and Lemuel and those who joined them.

chapters.n: Nephi sees his own people gathered in armies against the Lamanites. The final wars of Nephite history are coming into view.
The angel interprets more of Lehi’s dream: the filthy river is the depths of hell — a picture of spiritual separation from God.
The mists of darkness are the devil’s temptations. They blind eyes, harden hearts, and lead people onto “broad roads” where they become lost.

The great and spacious building is vain imagination and human pride. A terrible gulf separates it from the tree — the justice of God and the Messiah Himself stand between the proud and the blessings they reject.

f.g: Empty, self-centered thinking cut off from God.

f.w: a great and a terrible gulf

chapters.n: As the angel speaks, Nephi watches the Lamanites overpower his people. The reason is stated plainly: Nephite pride and the devil’s temptations.

f.w: because of the pride of my seed

chapters.n: The Lamanites overcome the Nephites and spread across the land.
Even after the Nephites are gone, wars continue for many generations among the survivors.
The angel warns that these people will “dwindle in unbelief” — gradually losing faith and the knowledge of the gospel.

Nephi describes the spiritual and social decline that follows lost faith. This language describes a condition of unbelief, not inherent worth. The Book of Mormon itself insists that all are alike unto God and promises a future restoration to these descendants.

f.g: Laziness; neglect of honest work.

chapters.n: The angel turns Nephi’s attention far into the future, beyond his own people, to many nations and kingdoms.
Again the angel teaches by asking Nephi to describe what he sees.
These are the nations of the Gentiles — peoples not of Israelite descent. Much of what follows concerns Europe and, later, the Americas.

f.g: In the Book of Mormon, usually non-Israelite nations, especially those from Europe who later settled the Americas.

chapters.n: Nephi sees a great “church” forming among the Gentiles. In this vision the word stands for any organization or system opposed to God, not one specific denomination.
The angel calls it the most abominable church because it persecutes, tortures, and enslaves God’s faithful people. A “yoke of iron” pictures harsh, unbreakable bondage.
Its true founder is the devil. Whatever form it takes, its source is opposition to God.

f.w: the devil that he was the founder of it

chapters.n: Nephi sees wealth, luxurious clothing, and harlots. These images, also found in Revelation, symbolize greed, worldliness, and immorality.

f.g: Expensive, finely woven linen fabric.

chapters.n: The angel explains that riches, fine clothing, and sexual sin are what this church truly desires — its goals are worldly, not godly.

f.w: the desires of this great and abominable church

chapters.n: It persecutes the saints in order to win the world’s praise. Seeking human approval at any cost is a mark of this church.

f.w: for the praise of the world

chapters.n: Nephi sees “many waters” — an ocean — separating the Gentile nations from his brothers’ descendants in the promised land.

f.g: The Atlantic Ocean separating Europe from the Americas.

chapters.n: The angel says God’s wrath is upon the Lamanite descendants because of their unbelief.

Nephi sees a man among the Gentiles, moved by the Spirit of God, who crosses the ocean to the promised land. Many Latter-day Saints, including Church leaders, have identified him as Christopher Columbus, who described feeling divinely led.

f.g: Commonly understood as Christopher Columbus (1492).
Worked upon; influenced and moved.

chapters.n: The Spirit moves other Gentiles too, and they leave “captivity” — often understood as the religious and political oppression of Europe — to cross the ocean. This fits colonists such as the Pilgrims seeking freedom.

f.w: they went forth out of captivity

chapters.n: Large numbers of Gentiles settle the promised land, and the descendants of Lehi’s people are scattered and struck down before them. Nephi sees, with sorrow, the suffering of native peoples.

f.w: scattered before the Gentiles and were smitten

chapters.n: The Gentile settlers prosper and take the land as their inheritance. Nephi compares their appearance to his own people before their destruction.

f.w: obtain the land for their inheritance

chapters.n: These settlers humble themselves before the Lord, and His power is with them.

f.w: did humble themselves before the Lord

chapters.n: Their “mother Gentiles” — the nations they came from — gather by land and sea to fight them. Many readers see the American Revolutionary War, when Britain fought its colonies.

f.g: The parent nations, especially Great Britain.

chapters.n: God’s power is with the colonists, and His wrath is upon those who fight against them.

f.w: the power of God was with them

chapters.n: Nephi sees the colonists delivered by God from all other nations — the birth of a free nation in the promised land.

f.w: delivered by the power of God

chapters.n: As they prosper, a book goes forth among them. This is the Bible, which was widely read in colonial America.

f.g: The Bible.

chapters.n: The angel asks whether Nephi knows what the book means.
Nephi admits he does not. His honesty invites further teaching.

The angel explains: it is a record of the Jews containing the Lord’s covenants with Israel and many prophecies. It resembles the brass plates Lehi’s family carried, though shorter, and it is of great worth to the Gentiles.

f.g: The Bible, especially the Old Testament.

chapters.n: When it first came from the Jews — including the writings of the apostles — the record contained the fulness of the gospel and testified truly of Christ.
At first these sacred writings passed in purity from the Jews to the Gentiles.

f.g: Uncorrupted and complete.

chapters.n: After the apostles carried the gospel to the Gentiles, the great and abominable church arose and removed many “plain and precious” parts of the gospel, including covenants. This is a key Book of Mormon teaching about why a restoration of truth was needed.
These changes were made on purpose — to twist the Lord’s ways and to blind and harden people.

f.w: pervert the right ways of the Lord

chapters.n: The angel summarizes: after the book passed through that church, many plain and precious things had been removed. Latter-day Saints believe the Bible is the word of God “as far as it is translated correctly,” and Joseph Smith’s inspired revision (JST) restored some lost material.

f.w: many plain and precious things taken away

chapters.n: This long verse explains the result: the Bible spreads to every Gentile nation, even to America, but because clear truths have been lost, a great many people stumble in confusion, and Satan gains great power over them.

f.w: plainness which is in the Lamb of God

chapters.n: Even so, the Lord will not allow the Gentiles in the promised land to wipe out Lehi’s descendants. The land was covenanted to Lehi’s family, and a mixed remnant of Nephite blood will survive among the Lamanites.

f.g: Nephite descendants who survived mixed among the Lamanites.

chapters.n: Nor will the Lord let the Gentiles destroy the Lamanites entirely.

f.w: destroy the seed of thy brethren

chapters.n: God will not leave the Gentiles forever in spiritual blindness caused by the lost truths. Help is coming.
Christ Himself speaks through the angel: He will show mercy to the Gentiles even while He judges the remnant of Israel.

f.w: I will be merciful unto the Gentiles

chapters.n: After Lehi’s descendants are judged and the Gentiles stumble, Christ promises to bring forth, by His own power, much more of His gospel in plain and precious form. Latter-day Saints see this as the Restoration, including the Book of Mormon.

Christ will show Himself to Nephi’s descendants, and they will write what He teaches. After their downfall, these records will be hidden, then brought forth to the Gentiles by the gift and power of God — exactly how the Book of Mormon describes its own origin.

f.w: I will manifest myself unto thy seed
by the gift and power of the Lamb

chapters.n: These records will contain Christ’s gospel, His “rock,” and His salvation — the sure foundation for faith.
Those who work to build Zion in that day will receive the Holy Ghost, and if they endure they will be saved. The last line quotes Isaiah: the feet of messengers bringing good news are beautiful.

f.g: The pure in heart; a people united in righteousness.

chapters.n: Nephi sees the Bible coming from the Gentiles to the remnant of his brothers’ descendants.

f.w: the book of the Lamb of God

chapters.n: Then “other books” come forth by Christ’s power — the Book of Mormon and other latter-day scripture — to convince Gentiles, Lehi’s descendants, and scattered Jews that the Bible’s prophets and apostles are true.
These last records will confirm the Bible, restore lost truths, and teach all people that Jesus is the Son of the Eternal Father and Savior of the world, and that all must come to Him to be saved.

f.w: shall establish the truth of the first

f.g: The Book of Mormon’s title page states the same purpose: to convince Jew and Gentile that Jesus is the Christ.

chapters.n: The Bible and the Book of Mormon will be “established in one.” Together they testify of the one God and one Shepherd over all the earth.

Christ will reveal Himself to all nations. The order reverses: in His mortal ministry the gospel went first to the Jews, then the Gentiles; in the last days it goes first to the Gentiles, then the Jews.

f.w: the last shall be first, and the first shall be last

chapters.n: The angel continues: if the Gentiles listen to Christ when He reveals Himself to them through His word and power in the last days, their “stumbling blocks” — the confusion caused by lost truths — will be removed.
Gentiles who accept Christ will be counted as Lehi’s descendants and as part of Israel — adopted into the covenant. They will be blessed in the promised land and no longer brought into captivity.

f.w: numbered among the house of Israel

f.g: Confused, put to shame, defeated.

chapters.n: The pit the devil’s church has dug to trap others will swallow those who dug it. This is a common scriptural principle: evil eventually destroys its makers. The “destruction” here is not annihilation of the soul but being cast into an endless hell.

f.w: shall be filled by those who digged it

chapters.n: This outcome is both the natural result of submitting to the devil’s captivity and the just judgment of God on those who choose wickedness.
The angel summarizes the lesson so far: repentant Gentiles will prosper, the Lord’s covenants with Israel will be kept, and those who refuse to repent must perish.
A warning: sorrow awaits the Gentiles if they harden their hearts against Christ.

f.g: Woe; grief or calamity — a prophetic warning cry.

chapters.n: Christ promises a “great and marvelous work” in the latter days — the Restoration of His gospel. It will have lasting effects either way: leading people to peace and eternal life, or leaving them to the blindness they choose.

f.w: a great and a marvelous work

chapters.n: The angel checks that Nephi remembers God’s covenants with Israel; Nephi says yes.
Nephi is shown the great and abominable church again, called the “mother of abominations,” founded by the devil.

In the end there are only two sides: the church of the Lamb and the church of the devil. This is not about denominations but allegiance — those who are not truly following Christ are, in effect, on the other side. The “whore” image depicts spiritual unfaithfulness.
Nephi sees her sitting on “many waters,” meaning she has power over many peoples and nations.
The church of the Lamb is small in numbers, but it exists across the whole earth. Its influence is limited by the great wickedness around it.

f.w: upon all the face of the earth

chapters.n: The forces of evil gather multitudes in every nation to fight against Christ and His people.

f.w: to fight against the Lamb of God

chapters.n: Yet Nephi sees God’s power descend on the Saints and the scattered covenant people. Their weapons are righteousness and the power of God, not worldly force.
God’s wrath falls on the abominable church, bringing wars and rumors of wars among all nations — the turmoil of the last days.
As these wars spread among nations aligned with evil, the angel tells Nephi that God’s judgment is falling on the “mother of harlots.”
When this judgment comes, the Father’s work of fulfilling His covenants with Israel will begin — the gathering of Israel in the last days.

f.w: the work of the Father shall commence

chapters.n: The angel calls Nephi to look once more.
Nephi sees a man in a white robe, a sign of purity and holiness.
The man is one of Christ’s twelve apostles.
This apostle will see and record the rest of these visions, and also things of the past.

f.w: write the remainder of these things

chapters.n: He will write about the end of the world — a description of the book of Revelation.
What this apostle writes is true. It is included in the Bible, which, when it first came from the Jews, was plain, pure, and easy for everyone to understand.

f.w: easy to the understanding of all men

chapters.n: Much of what the apostle will write overlaps with what Nephi has already seen; Nephi will also see the rest.
Nephi is forbidden to write what he sees next, because the Lord has assigned that writing to this apostle. God organizes His witnesses with purpose.
Other prophets have also seen all things and written them. Their records are sealed and will come forth in purity in the Lord’s own time. The brother of Jared is one such example.
The angel names the apostle: John, the beloved disciple and author of Revelation.
Nephi writes only a small part of what he saw. Restraint in sharing sacred experiences is a recurring theme in scripture.
Nephi testifies that he saw what his father saw — the answer to his prayer in 1 Nephi 11.

f.w: I saw the things which my father saw

chapters.n: Nephi closes his account of the vision: not everything is written, but what he has written is true.

f.w: the things which I have written are true

chapters.n: After his vision ends, Nephi returns to his father’s tent in the valley of Lemuel.
He finds Laman and Lemuel arguing about what Lehi had taught them.

f.g: Arguing; quarreling over meaning.

chapters.n: Lehi’s teachings were hard to understand unless a person asked the Lord. Because the brothers’ hearts were hard, they did not turn to God for help.

f.w: save a man should inquire of the Lord

chapters.n: Nephi grieves for two reasons: his brothers’ hard hearts and the future destruction he had just seen in vision.
Having seen his own people’s eventual fall, Nephi is overwhelmed with sorrow. He felt his afflictions were greater than anyone’s.
After regaining strength, Nephi asks his brothers what they are arguing about.
They say they cannot understand Lehi’s teachings about the natural branches of the olive tree and the Gentiles.

f.w: natural branches of the olive tree

chapters.n: Nephi asks the most important question: have they asked the Lord?

f.w: Have ye inquired of the Lord?

chapters.n: Their answer reveals the problem: they assume God doesn’t reveal things to people like them. Their unbelief keeps them from even asking.

f.w: the Lord maketh no such thing known unto us

chapters.n: Nephi gently challenges them: why don’t they keep God’s commandments? Why let their hard hearts lead them to spiritual ruin?
Nephi reminds them of the Lord’s promise: if they soften their hearts, ask in faith, and diligently keep the commandments, these truths will be made known. It is the formula for personal revelation.
Nephi explains the olive tree. Israel is the tree, and their family is a branch that has been broken off from it by leaving Jerusalem.

The grafting in will happen in the latter days, long after Christ’s mortal ministry and after their descendants have lost their faith. The full gospel will come to the Gentiles first, and then from the Gentiles to the remnant of Lehi’s seed.

At that time Lehi’s descendants will learn they belong to Israel and the covenant people, discover their ancestors’ story, and learn the gospel Christ taught their fathers — including the “very points of his doctrine” that show how to be saved. This describes the purpose of the Book of Mormon.
Nephi asks rhetorically: won’t they rejoice then, draw strength from the “true vine,” and come into God’s true fold? These are images of Christ as the source of life and of His flock.
Yes — Lehi’s descendants will be remembered and grafted back into the true olive tree as natural branches.
This will happen only after they are scattered by the Gentiles, and it will come through the Gentiles. Because the Jews rejected Christ, God will show His power to the Gentiles.

f.w: he shall be rejected of the Jews

chapters.n: Lehi’s prophecy applies to all Israel, fulfilling God’s covenant with Abraham that through his seed all the families of the earth would be blessed.

f.w: In thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed

chapters.n: Nephi also teaches his brothers about the restoration of the Jews in the last days.
He reads them Isaiah’s prophecies of Israel’s restoration — when they would no longer be confused or scattered. His patient teaching calms his brothers, and they humble themselves.

f.g: Calmed; made peaceful.

chapters.n: Now more open, the brothers ask what the tree in Lehi’s dream means.
Nephi says it represents the tree of life — linking the dream to the tree in Eden and to eternal life through God’s love.
They ask about the iron rod that led to the tree.
The rod is the word of God. Those who listen and hold fast to it will never perish, and the adversary’s “fiery darts” of temptation cannot blind them or lead them away.
Nephi pleads with all his energy that his brothers heed God’s word and always keep His commandments.

f.g: Ability or power of mind.

chapters.n: They ask what the river in the dream means.
Nephi explains it was filthy water. Lehi was so focused on other things — likely the joy of the fruit and his concern for his family — that he did not notice its filth.
The river is a terrible gulf separating the wicked from the tree of life and from the Saints.
It represents the awful hell prepared for the wicked.
Lehi also saw that God’s justice separates the wicked from the righteous. Its brightness is compared to an endless flaming fire that rises to God.
The brothers ask a thoughtful question: does this describe suffering in this life, the soul’s final state after death, or just earthly things?
Nephi answers that it represents both temporal and spiritual things, because everyone will be judged for what they do in this mortal life.

Those who die in wickedness will be cut off from spiritual blessings. At judgment, if their works were filthy, they remain filthy, and cannot live in God’s kingdom — otherwise His kingdom would become filthy too.
God’s kingdom is pure, and nothing unclean can enter it. So there must be a separate place for what remains unclean.

f.w: cannot any unclean thing enter into the kingdom of God

chapters.n: That place is hell, and the devil prepared it. In the end, people either live in God’s kingdom or are cast out by the justice Nephi described.

f.g: The one who prepared it.

chapters.n: The wicked are separated from the righteous and from the tree of life, whose fruit is the most precious and desirable — the greatest of all God’s gifts, which is eternal life.

f.w: the greatest of all the gifts of God

chapters.n: Laman and Lemuel complain that Nephi’s words are too harsh for them to bear. The truth about judgment felt like an attack on them.
Nephi replies that he spoke hard things only against wickedness, and he promised the righteous they would be lifted up. The guilty find truth hard because it cuts them to the core.

f.w: it cutteth them to the very center

chapters.n: If they were willing to hear and follow the truth, Nephi says, they wouldn’t complain that it was hard. Our reaction to truth often reveals the state of our hearts.

f.g: Complain under one’s breath; grumble in resentment.

chapters.n: Nephi earnestly urges his brothers to keep the Lord’s commandments.

f.g: Urge strongly; encourage.

chapters.n: For a time, the brothers humble themselves, and Nephi feels great joy and hope for them.
Nephi notes that all of this took place while the family camped in the valley of Lemuel.
Marriages unite the two families: Nephi, his brothers, and Zoram marry Ishmael’s daughters. Zoram, the former servant of Laban, marries the eldest — a sign he is fully part of the group.
Lehi had now done everything the Lord asked: secured the scriptures (brass plates) and brought Ishmael’s family for wives. Nephi feels richly blessed.
The Lord tells Lehi at night that the family must continue its journey the next day.
At his tent door Lehi finds a remarkable brass ball with two spindles; one points the direction to travel. It is later called the Liahona, meaning “compass.”

f.g: Skillfully and intricately made.

chapters.n: The family packs everything, including seeds of every kind — they are preparing to farm in a new land.
They break camp and cross the river Laman, heading into the wilderness.
After four days traveling south-southeast, they camp at a place they name Shazer.

f.g: Meaning uncertain; some suggest a Semitic word related to trees or a place of palms.

chapters.n: They hunt for food with bows and arrows and continue along the most fertile strip of land near the Red Sea — likely the coastal region of western Arabia.
They travel many days, hunting with bows, arrows, and slings to survive.
The ball guides them through the more fertile areas — God leads them where they can find food.
After many days of travel they stop to rest and get food.
Disaster: Nephi breaks his fine steel bow, and since the others’ bows have also failed, the families have no way to get food. His brothers are angry with him.

f.g: Hardened metal; ancient “steel” could refer to strong iron alloys.

chapters.n: The hunters return empty-handed to exhausted, hungry families.

f.g: Because they lacked food.

chapters.n: Laman, Lemuel, and Ishmael’s sons complain bitterly. Strikingly, even Lehi murmurs against the Lord — a reminder that prophets are human and can struggle under pressure.
With the other bows’ springs gone slack, finding food becomes nearly impossible.

f.g: Lost their tension or flexibility, making them useless.

chapters.n: Nephi speaks to his brothers, whose hearts have hardened again to the point of complaining against God.

Instead of complaining, Nephi makes a new bow from wood and an arrow from a straight stick. Then, though he could have asked God directly, he goes to his father for direction — honoring Lehi’s role even after Lehi faltered.

f.w: Whither shall I go to obtain food?

chapters.n: Lehi asks the Lord. Nephi notes that his words had helped the family humble themselves.
The Lord answers Lehi and corrects him for murmuring. Lehi is deeply humbled and sorrowful.

f.g: Corrected and disciplined, with a view to improvement.

chapters.n: The Lord tells Lehi to look at the ball and read what is written on it.
What Lehi reads makes him and the whole family tremble with fear — likely a sobering message about their murmuring.
Nephi observes a key principle: the pointers worked according to their faith, diligence, and attention.

f.w: according to the faith and diligence

chapters.n: New writing would appear on the ball, changing over time as their faith changed. Nephi draws the lesson: by small means the Lord brings about great things. Alma later compares the Liahona to the words of Christ.

f.w: by small means the Lord can bring about great things

chapters.n: Following the ball’s directions, Nephi climbs to the top of a mountain.
There he finds and kills wild animals — enough food for the families.

f.g: Wild game animals.

chapters.n: The families rejoice when Nephi returns with food. They humble themselves and thank the Lord.
The journey resumes in nearly the same direction, and they later camp again for a time.
Ishmael dies and is buried at Nahom. Ancient altars found in Yemen bear the tribal name NHM from about this period, which many scholars see as a notable connection to this place name.

f.g: Possibly from a Hebrew root meaning “to mourn” or “comfort.” An NHM tribal region is attested in southern Arabia.

chapters.n: Ishmael’s daughters mourn deeply and blame Lehi for bringing them out of Jerusalem only to suffer hunger, thirst, and exhaustion. Their grief is real, and their complaint is human.
They complain against both Lehi and Nephi and want to return to Jerusalem.

f.w: desirous to return again to Jerusalem

chapters.n: Laman proposes murdering Lehi and Nephi. He resents his younger brother leading and teaching the older ones — echoing the resentment Joseph’s brothers felt in Genesis.
Laman accuses Nephi of lying about revelations and using tricks to seize power and make himself king. These accusations would echo through Lamanite tradition for centuries.

f.g: Clever tricks or deceptions.

chapters.n: The Lord intervenes, speaking directly to the rebels and sharply rebuking them. They repent, and the Lord blesses the family with food again.

f.w: the voice of the Lord came

chapters.n: From Nahom the family turns nearly eastward, traveling through great hardship. Children are born along the way.

f.g: Many researchers trace this turn across southern Arabia toward the coast of present-day Oman.

chapters.n: God blesses them so much that even living on raw meat, the mothers have plenty of milk and become as strong as the men, and they stop complaining.

f.g: Nurse their babies with ample milk.

chapters.n: Nephi draws a lesson: God’s commands will be fulfilled, and when people obey, He nourishes, strengthens, and provides a way to do what He asks.

f.w: provide means whereby they can accomplish

chapters.n: Their wilderness journey lasts eight years.

They reach a fertile land by the sea, full of fruit and wild honey, which they name Bountiful. They call the sea Irreantum, “many waters.” Researchers have identified plausible sites on the coast of southern Oman.

f.g: Named for its abundance; distinct from a later Nephite land of the same name.
Nephi translates it as “many waters” — likely the Arabian Sea / Indian Ocean.

chapters.n: After years of hardship too many to record, the family rejoices to camp at the seashore.
After many days in Bountiful, the Lord calls Nephi up a mountain, and Nephi prays there.
The Lord commands Nephi to build a ship according to a pattern He will show, to carry the family across the ocean.

f.w: after the manner which I shall show thee

chapters.n: Nephi doesn’t ask whether he can do it — only where to find ore so he can make tools. His faith goes straight to action.

f.g: Metal-bearing rock to melt (smelt) into usable metal.

chapters.n: The Lord shows Nephi where to find ore.
Nephi makes a bellows from animal skins to blast air into the fire, and starts a fire by striking stones together.

f.g: A bag that pumps air into a fire to make it hot enough to smelt metal.

chapters.n: Nephi explains that the Lord had not allowed them to make much fire in the wilderness — perhaps to avoid drawing attention — but promised to make their uncooked food taste good.

f.w: I will make thy food become sweet

chapters.n: God promised to be their light and to prepare their way, as long as they obeyed. Their safe arrival would show them it was God leading them.

f.w: I will also be your light

chapters.n: Arriving in the promised land would prove that the Lord is God, that He saved them from Jerusalem’s destruction, and that He led them out.

f.w: ye shall know that I, the Lord, am God

chapters.n: Because of these promises, Nephi tries to keep the commandments and urges his brothers to be faithful.
Nephi smelts the ore and forges tools.

f.g: Melted and extracted from the rock.

chapters.n: Seeing Nephi preparing to build a ship, his brothers mock him as a fool who thinks he can cross the ocean.
The brothers refuse to help. They don’t believe Nephi can build a ship or that God is instructing him.

f.w: desirous that they might not labor
f.g: Did not want to work.

chapters.n: When Nephi grows sorrowful over their hard hearts, they gloat, saying they knew he lacked the judgment for such a great work.

f.g: Lacking good sense.

chapters.n: They insult Lehi as a foolish dreamer, recount the women’s suffering in childbirth in the wilderness, and claim the women would have been better off dying in Jerusalem.

f.g: Heavily pregnant.

chapters.n: They mourn the comfortable life they might have had with their property in Jerusalem. Their focus is on lost comfort, not on God’s purposes.
They claim the people of Jerusalem were righteous because they kept the law of Moses, and that Lehi unfairly judged them. But Jeremiah and other prophets of the time said otherwise.

f.w: the people who were in the land of Jerusalem were a righteous people

f.g: Laws and legal decisions of the law of Moses.

chapters.n: Nephi answers with Israel’s own history: would their ancestors have escaped Egypt if they had ignored the Lord’s word?

f.w: led away out of the hands of the Egyptians

chapters.n: Would Israel have been freed if God had not commanded Moses to lead them? Nephi compares Lehi to Moses.
Israel’s bondage was cruel and their labor crushing, so their deliverance was clearly good.
Moses was commanded to do the work, and by his word the Red Sea parted and Israel walked through on dry ground.

f.w: the waters of the Red Sea were divided

chapters.n: Pharaoh’s armies drowned in the Red Sea.
God fed Israel with manna in the wilderness — just as He has fed this family.

f.g: Bread-like food God gave Israel daily in the wilderness.

chapters.n: Moses struck the rock by God’s power, and water flowed for thirsty Israel.

Even with God leading them by day and night, the Israelites hardened their hearts and spoke against Moses and God. Nephi is holding up a mirror to his brothers. He also identifies the God who led Israel as their Redeemer.

f.w: the Lord their God, their Redeemer
leading them by day and giving light unto them by night

chapters.n: Everything — destroying the wicked, leading Israel, providing for them — happened by God’s word.
After crossing the Jordan, God gave Israel power to drive out the land’s inhabitants.
Nephi asks: were the Canaanites driven out because they were righteous? No.

f.g: The Canaanite peoples.

chapters.n: Nor were the Israelites chosen because they were inherently better. If the Canaanites had been righteous, they would have been just as choice.

A powerful principle: the Lord values all people equally, and favors the righteous. The Canaanites had rejected God and were “ripe in iniquity,” so the land was cursed for them and blessed for Israel.

f.w: the Lord esteemeth all flesh in one

f.g: Fully ready for judgment, like fruit ready to harvest.

chapters.n: God created the earth to be lived on, and He created His children to inherit it.

f.w: created the earth that it should be inhabited

chapters.n: God raises up righteous nations and brings down wicked ones.
He leads the righteous to precious lands and curses lands for the wicked — exactly what is happening to Lehi’s family as they leave a doomed Jerusalem.
God reigns from heaven, with the earth as His footstool — an image of His supreme power.
God loves those who accept Him as their God. Because of His covenants with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, He brought Israel out of Egypt.

Because Israel hardened their hearts, God disciplined them. When poisonous serpents bit them, He provided healing — they only had to look at a brass serpent on a pole. Because it was so simple, many refused and died. The serpent is a symbol of Christ.

f.g: To restrict or put in hardship; to discipline.

chapters.n: Israel kept hardening their hearts and reviling Moses and God, yet God’s matchless power still brought them to the promised land.

f.g: Speak abusively against.

chapters.n: Now Jerusalem has become wicked, nearly ripe for destruction. Nephi suspects it may be destroyed even now, except for a few taken captive.
That’s why Lehi was commanded to leave. Nephi boldly points out that Laman and Lemuel, like the Jews who sought Lehi’s life, have also wanted to kill their father — making them murderers at heart.
A famous verse: Laman and Lemuel are quick to sin and slow to remember God. They had seen an angel and heard God’s “still small voice,” but they were “past feeling,” so God had to speak like thunder.
They know God’s word can make the earth pass away and reshape the land. How, then, can their hearts be so hard?

f.w: rough places to be made smooth

chapters.n: Nephi’s soul is torn with anguish; he fears his brothers will be cast off forever. He is so full of the Spirit that his body loses strength.

Furious, the brothers try to throw Nephi into the sea. He commands them in God’s name not to touch him, warning that he is so filled with divine power that anyone who touches him will wither like a dried reed.

f.w: wither even as a dried reed

chapters.n: Nephi commands them to stop murmuring against their father and to help build the ship.
With God, Nephi says, he could do anything God commanded — even turn water into earth.
If God has worked so many miracles, surely He can teach Nephi to build a ship.

f.g: Worked, performed.

chapters.n: Nephi’s words leave his brothers speechless. For many days they dare not touch him for fear of withering, so strong is the Spirit.

f.g: Dared.
Confused, unable to answer.

chapters.n: The Lord tells Nephi to stretch out his hand to his brothers: they will not wither, but God will “shock” them so they know He is the Lord.

f.g: Give them a sudden jolt of divine power.

chapters.n: Nephi stretches out his hand, and the Lord shakes the brothers as promised.
Convinced, the brothers fall at Nephi’s feet to worship him. Nephi refuses: he is only their younger brother. They should worship God and honor their parents — quoting the fifth commandment.

f.w: honor thy father and thy mother

chapters.n: Humbled, the brothers worship the Lord and help Nephi. They shape timbers with skill, and the Lord shows Nephi step by step how to work them.
Nephi emphasizes that the ship was built not by human methods but the way the Lord showed him. Its design came from revelation.

f.w: not after the manner of men

chapters.n: Nephi often went to the mountain to pray, and the Lord showed him great things. His revelation came through steady, repeated seeking.

f.w: I did pray oft unto the Lord

chapters.n: When the ship is finished, even the brothers see its excellent craftsmanship and humble themselves again.

f.g: Of very high quality.

chapters.n: The Lord tells Lehi it is time to board the ship.
The family loads fruit, meat, abundant honey, provisions, and seeds, then boards in order of age with their wives and children.

f.w: every one according to his age
f.g: In order by age — perhaps reflecting family rank or careful order.

chapters.n: Lehi and Sariah had two sons born in the wilderness: Jacob, the elder, and Joseph. Both become important later — Jacob as a prophet and record keeper.
They set sail, driven by the wind toward the promised land.

After many days, Laman, Lemuel, Ishmael’s sons and their wives begin partying with rude, crude behavior, forgetting the power that brought them there. The problem is not celebration itself but forgetting God.

f.g: Coarse, vulgar, disrespectful behavior.

chapters.n: Nephi fears God will be angry and they will sink. When he soberly warns them, they angrily refuse to have their younger brother rule over them.

f.g: Seriousness and earnestness.

chapters.n: Laman and Lemuel tie Nephi up and treat him harshly. The Lord allows this in order to show His power and fulfill His word concerning the wicked.

f.g: The Lord allowed it.

chapters.n: Once Nephi is bound and cannot move, the Liahona stops working. The compass functions by faith, and rebellion shuts it down.
Without direction, a great storm drives the ship backward for three days. The brothers are terrified, yet still refuse to untie Nephi.

f.g: Violent storm.
Untie, set free.

chapters.n: On the fourth day the storm becomes extremely violent.

f.g: Severe, intense.

chapters.n: About to sink, the brothers finally realize God’s judgments are on them and they will perish unless they repent. They untie Nephi, whose wrists and ankles are badly swollen.

f.w: swallowed up in the depths of the sea

chapters.n: Despite great pain, Nephi praises God all day and does not complain. His response to suffering is a model of faith.

f.w: I did praise him all the day long

chapters.n: Lehi pleaded with the rebels, but they threatened anyone who defended Nephi. Lehi and Sariah, now elderly and grief-stricken over their children, fell ill.

f.g: Advanced in age.
