chapters.n: Their grief nearly killed them. Nephi’s poetic language — grey hairs brought down to the dust, a watery grave — echoes Jacob’s mourning in Genesis.

f.w: their grey hairs were about to be brought down

chapters.n: Young Jacob and Joseph suffered seeing their mother’s affliction. Nephi’s wife and children wept and prayed, but nothing softened the brothers’ hearts.

f.w: my wife with her tears and prayers

chapters.n: Only the threat of destruction by God’s power softened them. Facing death, they repented and released Nephi.
Once free, Nephi takes the compass and it works again. He prays, and the storm stops; a great calm follows — echoing Jesus calming the sea.
Nephi steers the ship back on course toward the promised land.
After many days they reach the promised land, go ashore, pitch their tents, and name it “the promised land.” Its exact location is not specified.
They farm the land, planting the seeds brought from Jerusalem, and the crops grow abundantly.

Exploring, they find many animals and ores of gold, silver, and copper. Nephi names animals using the words familiar to him; scholars discuss how some terms may have been applied to similar local creatures.
Commanded by the Lord, Nephi makes metal plates to record his people’s history — Lehi’s record, their journey, and many prophecies. These first plates are known as the large plates of Nephi.
Nephi explains that when he made the first plates he didn’t yet know he would be told to make a second set. So the detailed history and genealogy are on the first (large) plates.

f.g: The large plates — mainly history.

chapters.n: Later, commanded again, Nephi made “these plates” — the small plates — for the ministry and prophecies, especially the plain and precious parts. They were kept for his people and for “wise purposes” known to the Lord. One such purpose became clear when the 116 manuscript pages were lost in 1828.
The other plates record more of the wars and destructions. Nephi commanded that these plates be passed down from prophet to prophet.

f.w: handed down from one generation to another

chapters.n: Nephi promises to tell later about making these plates; his goal is to preserve the most sacred things.

f.w: an account of my making these plates

chapters.n: Nephi writes only what he considers sacred. If he errs, he says, it is from human weakness — and prophets of old erred too.
What some people treasure, others trample. Many even treat God Himself as worthless and refuse His counsel.

f.g: Treat him as worthless.

chapters.n: Nephi repeats the angel’s timeline: Christ will come six hundred years after Lehi left Jerusalem.
The world will treat Him as nothing. He will be whipped, struck, and spat upon — and He will endure it out of loving kindness and patience toward humanity.

f.g: Whip, flog.
Patient endurance.

chapters.n: A key teaching: the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — who led Israel out of Egypt — is the one who will be crucified. Nephi cites three prophets on the brass plates: Zenock, Neum, and Zenos, whose writings are not in our Bible.

f.w: the God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and the God of Jacob

chapters.n: Zenos foresaw that when Christ died, the Lord would visit Israel: the righteous by His voice, others by thunder, fire, darkness, earthquakes, and upheaval. This matches events in 3 Nephi 8–10.
Zenos foretold that as the earth groaned and rocks split, many kings of distant lands would be moved to cry out: “The God of nature suffers.”

f.g: In Hebrew idiom, distant coastlands — lands far across the sea.

chapters.n: The prophet also foresaw that the people of Jerusalem, having crucified the God of Israel and rejected His signs, would suffer at the hands of all nations.

Because they despised the Holy One of Israel, they would wander, be mocked and hated among the nations. Sadly, history has seen much persecution of Jewish people, which latter-day scripture condemns while affirming God’s love for them.

f.g: An object of scorn and a proverb of ridicule.

chapters.n: But when they stop turning away from the Holy One of Israel, He will remember His covenants with their fathers.

f.w: then will he remember the covenants

chapters.n: God will remember the isles of the sea and gather all Israel from the four corners of the earth, according to Zenos.
All the earth will see the Lord’s salvation, and every people will be blessed.

f.w: all the earth shall see the salvation of the Lord

chapters.n: Nephi explains his purpose: to persuade his people to remember the Lord their Redeemer.
He addresses his words to all Israel, wherever they might receive them.
Nephi is so burdened by spiritual concern for the people of Jerusalem that it wearies him physically. Had the Lord not warned his family, they would have perished too.

f.g: Intense spiritual feelings or burdens.

chapters.n: God showed ancient prophets everything about Jerusalem, and many prophesied of Lehi’s people too. Those prophecies are on the brass plates.
Nephi reads to his brothers from the brass plates so they can learn how God dealt with people in other lands and times.

Nephi reads the books of Moses, but to persuade them more fully to believe in Christ, he reads Isaiah. He “likens” all scripture to them — applying it to their own lives. This is a key principle for scripture study.

f.w: I did liken all scriptures unto us

f.g: The first five books of the Bible (Genesis–Deuteronomy).

chapters.n: Nephi invites his family, a broken-off branch of Israel, to hear Isaiah’s words to all Israel and apply them, so they can share the hope of their scattered kin. The next two chapters quote Isaiah 48–49.

f.w: a branch who have been broken off

chapters.n: Nephi quotes Isaiah 48 from the brass plates. Isaiah addresses Israel’s people, who claim God’s name but don’t worship Him sincerely. Nephi’s version adds “or out of the waters of baptism,” a phrase Joseph Smith added in the 1840 edition to clarify the meaning of “waters of Judah.”

f.g: Israel; Jacob was renamed Israel.
Not in the KJV; added in the 1840 Book of Mormon edition.
KJV reads “but not in truth.” They make oaths by God without meaning them.

chapters.n: They proudly call themselves citizens of the holy city, Jerusalem, yet do not rely on God. The Book of Mormon says they “do not stay themselves” on God, where the KJV says they “stay themselves” — making clear their trust is hollow.

f.g: Lean on, rely on.
Hebrew YHWH Tseva’ot — the Lord of the armies of heaven.

chapters.n: God reminds Israel that He announced past events long before they happened, then suddenly brought them to pass. Fulfilled prophecy shows He is the true God.
He foretold events in advance because Israel was stubborn. A neck like iron and a forehead of brass picture rigid, unbending pride.

f.w: thy neck is an iron sinew
f.g: Stiff-necked: refusing to bow, like an ox resisting the yoke.
A hard, shameless forehead.

chapters.n: God told them ahead of time so they couldn’t credit their idols for what He had done.

f.g: An idol carved from wood or stone; a “molten image” is cast from metal.

chapters.n: They have seen and heard it all — will they not testify? Now God reveals new, hidden things. The Book of Mormon reads “seen and heard” where the KJV has “heard, see.”
These new things were not known before, so Israel cannot claim it already knew them.

f.w: lest thou shouldst say—Behold I knew them
f.g: God prevents Israel from taking credit for His revelations.

chapters.n: Israel did not listen or understand; their ears were closed. God knew they would act treacherously; from their beginnings they were rebels.
Yet for His own name’s sake God holds back His anger and does not destroy them. His mercy rests on His character, not their merit.

f.g: Delay, hold back.

chapters.n: God has refined Israel in the “furnace of affliction,” like metal purified by fire. The Book of Mormon omits the KJV’s phrase “but not with silver.” Trials can be a means of choosing and purifying God’s people.

God acts for His own sake and will not let His name be dishonored or share His glory with idols. The Book of Mormon’s “I will not suffer my name to be polluted” replaces the KJV’s question “how should my name be polluted?”

f.w: I will not give my glory unto another

chapters.n: God calls Israel to listen: He is the first and the last, eternal and unchanging. Latter-day Saints understand the speaker, Jehovah, to be the premortal Jesus Christ, who uses the same title in Revelation.

f.w: I am the first, and I am also the last

chapters.n: God’s hand laid the earth’s foundation and stretched out the heavens; when He calls, creation stands at attention.

f.g: Measured or stretched out the sky with His hand.

chapters.n: Which idol predicted this? The Lord has chosen someone to carry out His will against Babylon and the Chaldeans — historically Cyrus of Persia, who conquered Babylon in 539 BC. The Book of Mormon adds that God will fulfill the word declared by His prophets.

f.g: The ruling people of the Neo-Babylonian empire.

f.w: he will do his pleasure on Babylon

chapters.n: The Lord has called this deliverer and will make his mission succeed.
God has spoken openly from the beginning, not in secret. The speaker says the Lord God and His Spirit have sent him — words many see as pointing to a prophet or to the Messiah.

f.w: I have not spoken in secret

chapters.n: The Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, teaches His people what is truly good and leads them in the right way.

f.w: thy Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel

f.g: Teaches you what is truly for your benefit.

chapters.n: A tender lament: if only Israel had obeyed, their peace would have flowed like a river and their righteousness rolled in like ocean waves — steady and endless.

f.w: thy peace been as a river

chapters.n: Their descendants would have been as countless as sand, and their name would never have been cut off — the Abrahamic promise fulfilled.

f.g: Your own children; “bowels” was a KJV way of saying “body” or “inner parts.”

chapters.n: A joyful command: leave Babylon, flee the Chaldeans, and proclaim to the whole earth that the Lord has redeemed Israel. In the latter days “Babylon” also symbolizes worldliness that God’s people must flee.
Just as God gave water from the rock in the Exodus, He will care for those returning home through the desert.

f.w: waters to flow out of the rock

f.g: Split open.

chapters.n: Despite all God has done — the Book of Mormon adds “and greater also” — the wicked will find no peace.

f.w: there is no peace, saith the Lord, unto the wicked

chapters.n: Nephi continues with Isaiah 49. The Book of Mormon has a longer opening than the KJV, addressing scattered Israel “broken off” because of wicked leaders — words that fit Lehi’s family well. Then the Servant speaks: the Lord called him before birth.

f.g: Shepherds — here, Israel’s religious and political leaders.
KJV Isaiah 49:1 begins here; the earlier words are unique to the Book of Mormon.

chapters.n: The Servant’s words are like a sharp sword, and God has kept him hidden like a polished arrow in a quiver, ready for the right moment.

f.g: A well-made arrow.

chapters.n: God calls the Servant “Israel,” through whom He will be glorified. The Servant can be understood as Israel as a people, a prophet, and ultimately Jesus Christ, the perfect Servant.
The Servant feels his labor has been in vain, yet trusts that God will judge and reward his work. Many faithful servants feel this discouragement.
Though Israel is not yet gathered, the Servant will be honored by the Lord, who will be his strength.

f.w: to bring Jacob again to him

chapters.n: Restoring Israel is too small a task: the Servant will also be a light to the Gentiles, bringing God’s salvation to the ends of the earth.
The Servant, despised and hated by the nations, will one day be honored by kings and princes who rise and bow. The Book of Mormon reads “to servant of rulers” (KJV “to a servant of rulers”).

In a time of favor God helps His people and gives His Servant as a covenant to restore desolate lands. The Book of Mormon adds “O isles of the sea” and “my servant,” making clear that the scattered remnants, like Lehi’s family, are included.
The Servant will free prisoners and call those in darkness into the light — an image Latter-day Saints also connect with Christ’s work for the dead.

f.w: say to the prisoners: Go forth

chapters.n: Those returning will never hunger or thirst. Their merciful Shepherd will lead them to springs of water.

f.w: They shall not hunger nor thirst

chapters.n: God will turn the mountains into roads and raise up highways for the gathering.
Israel will be gathered from far away: north, west, and the land of Sinim.

f.g: A distant land; some scholars link it to Syene (Aswan) in southern Egypt, others to China.

chapters.n: Heaven and earth are invited to sing because God comforts His people. The Book of Mormon adds that those in the east will be established and “smitten no more.”
Zion feels abandoned and forgotten. The Book of Mormon adds a reassurance: “but he will show that he hath not.”
One of scripture’s most tender images: even if a nursing mother could forget her baby, God will never forget Israel. The Book of Mormon adds “O house of Israel.”

f.w: can a woman forget her sucking child

chapters.n: God has engraved Israel on the palms of His hands. Christians see a reminder of Christ’s nail-scarred hands, which He showed to His disciples after the Resurrection.

f.w: graven thee upon the palms of my hands

chapters.n: Zion’s children will hurry home, and those who destroyed her will leave.

f.g: Hurry; the Hebrew can also mean “builders,” a play on words.

chapters.n: Look around: Zion’s children are gathering. She will wear them like ornaments or a bride’s jewelry.
Zion’s ruined land will become too crowded for all its people, and her enemies will be far away.

f.w: too narrow by reason of the inhabitants

chapters.n: The children born after Zion’s losses will say the land is too cramped and ask for more room.

f.g: Too narrow, cramped.

chapters.n: Zion, amazed, asks where all these children came from when she had been bereaved, captive, and alone.

f.g: Wandering as an exile.

chapters.n: God will raise His banner to the Gentiles, who will carry Israel’s sons and daughters home. Nephi explains in the next chapter that this means Gentile nations helping gather Israel.

f.g: Raise a banner or flag as a rallying point.

chapters.n: Kings and queens will become Israel’s caretakers. Bowing low depicts honoring Israel, and those who wait for the Lord will never be ashamed.

f.w: they shall not be ashamed that wait for me

chapters.n: A question: can captives be taken from a mighty warrior? Normally, no.

f.g: Captives held by a powerful or rightful captor.

chapters.n: But God will free even the captives of the mighty. He will fight those who fight Israel and save her children.

f.w: I will contend with him that contendeth with thee

chapters.n: Israel’s oppressors will destroy one another — a vivid poetic picture of self-destructive evil. Then all will know that the Lord is Israel’s Savior and Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob.

f.w: feed them that oppress thee with their own flesh

chapters.n: After hearing Isaiah, Nephi’s brothers ask a sincere question: are these prophecies only spiritual, or will they happen literally? It is a sign of progress that they ask at all.
Nephi explains that the Spirit revealed these things to Isaiah, and the Spirit shows prophets what will actually happen to people “according to the flesh” — that is, in real life.

f.w: by the Spirit are all things made known

chapters.n: The prophecies are both temporal and spiritual. Israel will literally be scattered across the earth among every nation.

f.w: scattered upon all the face of the earth

chapters.n: Many Israelites are already lost to those at Jerusalem — most of the tribes were taken away (by Assyria, about 722 BC) and scattered. No one knows exactly where they went. These are often called the lost ten tribes.

f.w: the more part of all the tribes have been led away

chapters.n: The prophecies apply to these lost tribes and to all who will later be scattered for hardening their hearts against the Holy One of Israel. They will be hated among the nations.
Nephi interprets Isaiah 49:22–23: the Gentiles nursing Israel and carrying her children are literal, temporal events. They apply to Lehi’s descendants and all Israel in the future.

f.g: Banner or rallying flag.

chapters.n: After Israel is scattered, God will raise a mighty Gentile nation in this very land — the Americas — and that nation will scatter Lehi’s descendants. Many see this as the United States.

f.w: a mighty nation among the Gentiles

chapters.n: Then God will do a “marvelous work” among the Gentiles that will greatly bless Lehi’s descendants — the restoration of the gospel and the coming forth of the Book of Mormon. This is how the Gentiles “carry” Israel.
This work will bless Gentiles and all Israel, revealing the covenants made to Abraham that through his seed all the earth would be blessed.

f.w: In thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed

chapters.n: The world can only be blessed if God “makes bare His arm” — rolls up His sleeve, so to speak, and shows His power openly.

f.g: Roll back the sleeve to act with full strength.

chapters.n: God will show His power to all nations by bringing His covenants and gospel to Israel.

f.w: in the eyes of all the nations

chapters.n: Israel will be freed from captivity, gathered to their promised lands, brought out of spiritual darkness, and will know the Lord as their Savior and Redeemer.

f.w: out of obscurity and out of darkness

chapters.n: Nephi explains Isaiah 49:26: the great and abominable church will turn on itself; its violence will come back on its own head.
Nations that fight Israel will turn on each other and fall into the pit they dug for God’s people. All who fight Zion will be destroyed, and the great and abominable church will collapse.

Satan will soon lose his power over people’s hearts. The proud and wicked will be like stubble that is burned — dry leftover stalks, quickly consumed. Nephi quotes a prophet whose words also appear later in Malachi.

f.g: The dry stalks left after harvest.

chapters.n: God’s full wrath will be poured out on the wicked, because He will not allow them to destroy the righteous.

f.w: fulness of the wrath of God

chapters.n: Even if fire must destroy their enemies, God will preserve the righteous by His power. The righteous need not fear: they will be saved, “even as by fire.”

f.w: saved, even if it so be as by fire

chapters.n: Blood, fire, and smoke will come upon the earth for those who harden their hearts against the Holy One of Israel.

f.w: blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke

chapters.n: The righteous will not perish, but all who fight against Zion will be cut off.
Nephi cites Moses’ prophecy that God would raise up a prophet like Moses; whoever refuses to hear Him will be cut off.

f.w: A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you, like unto me

chapters.n: Nephi identifies that prophet: the Holy One of Israel — Jesus Christ — who will judge in righteousness. The New Testament and Christ Himself (in 3 Nephi) say the same.

f.w: this prophet of whom Moses spake was the Holy One of Israel

chapters.n: The righteous need not fear and will not be put to shame. It is the devil’s kingdom, established among mortals, that is in danger.

Nephi describes the kingdom of the devil: churches built for money, power, or popularity; and all who seek fleshly lusts, worldly things, and iniquity. They are the ones who should tremble — they will be consumed like stubble.

f.w: popular in the eyes of the world

chapters.n: The righteous will be led up like calves from the stall — well fed and leaping with joy — and the Holy One of Israel will reign in glory.

f.g: Calves kept and fed in a barn; once released they leap for joy.

chapters.n: The Good Shepherd gathers His children from every corner of the earth. His sheep know Him, and there will be one fold and one shepherd.
Because His people are righteous, Satan will have no power and will be bound for many years — the Millennium. Satan is bound because the people’s own righteousness gives him no place in their hearts.

f.w: he cannot be loosed for the space of many years

chapters.n: Nephi repeats: all these things will literally happen.
Every nation and people can be safe in the Holy One of Israel — if they repent. The invitation is universal.

f.w: if it so be that they will repent

chapters.n: Nephi stops here; he does not yet dare say more about these things.

f.g: Dared.

chapters.n: Nephi asks his brothers to consider that the brass plates are true and teach that a person must obey God’s commandments.

Lehi and Nephi are not the only witnesses — many prophets have taught the same. Nephi ends the first book with a simple promise: keep the commandments and endure to the end, and you will be saved at the last day.
